utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as always, I'm going to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are about to resume your examination-in-chief. Once again, I have to ask you that we both try not to overlap. Furthermore, it would be useful as far as possible to take into account the protective measures you were granted, especially in terms of your position, your job at the time, or anything else that might reveal your identity as a protected witness. Whenever necessary, we shall be going into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we'll need to redact this question. I just warned the witness and I was the first transgressor today. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It happens to the best of us, Mr. Milovancevic. Okay. Can we please redact line 25 of page 1 and line 1 of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked about your arrival in the public security station in Benkovac early in April 1991. You described the situation on the ground as a war. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the decision was taken to send in the blue helmets, I mean UN troops, to the former Yugoslavia, the force usually referred to as UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the specific date when the decision was adopted by the UN Security Council, when the decision was adopted to send peacekeeping troops to the former Yugoslavia. I do know, however, that these units comprised a military component as well as a number of civilian police. They arrived sometime early in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps know what the basic condition was for UN deployment in the area? What sort of situation on the ground did that require for the UN troops to arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the principal condition for the arrival of the UN troops was a cease-fire between the warring parties. That is the JNA and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how the clashes continued? Who was attacking whom? You said there was a war on. Obviously there were clashes. So, in short, who was attacking whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I arrived in Benkovac municipality and just after, which means sometime in April and May 1992, positions were attacked that were being held by the JNA. These positions were being attacked by the Croatian army. I'm talking about positions around Zemunik airport, Kotik [phoen], Babin Dub and several other elevations in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt a little bit, Mr. Milovancevic? Sorry, Witness, is your headphone okay? Can you hear well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have described the situation you found when you arrived in the Benkovac public security station. You say the situation was difficult. Can you provide more detail? Can you describe more specifically the situation you found in the station or in the area covered by that police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said the situation in the station itself as well as in Benkovac municipality was difficult, first and foremost what I had in mind was the situation concerning daily combat throughout the municipality. Settled areas were being shelled as well as the town of Benkovac itself. What made the situation even more difficult was the large number of refugees who found refuge in Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was that was shelling the settled areas and which refugees are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling of the town of Benkovac itself and those settled areas was being done by the Croatian army. As for the refugees, those were Serbs who fled from a range of coastal towns, Zadar, Biograd, the area around Biograd, where a great number of Serbs used to live, but now in 1991 and 1992, they fled to Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who had been chief of the Benkovac public security station prior to your arrival? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosko Drazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please go into private session for a moment, Your Honour, due to the nature of some of the questions to follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In one of your previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I think I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are already in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In one of your previous answers, Witness, you said that sometime around April or May the UN troops arrived as well as a number of UN civilian police. Did that bring about any changes in the way the public security station in Benkovac was organised, was structured, in the work of the local SUP, the Krajina SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More throughout May and June 1992. That was when the military component of the UN started deploying with greater intensity and the clashes abated. The civilian police had just reorganised in Benkovac itself somewhat earlier. We then started to work with them, especially with the civilian police, since due to the nature of our work we had closer ties with them, whereas the military was cooperating more with the military component of the UN troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was for the most part in May and June that the UN troops deployed in the area. What's happening to the JNA at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, the decision was made for the Yugoslav People's Army to withdraw towards the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from there, to go on withdrawing to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That meant that all active-duty troops who were not natives of Croatia were leaving, together with a great number of officers who were not natives of Croatia. All of them would be leaving the area, taking with them the greatest part of the military equipment and materiel, the logistical support and documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was going on with the weapons of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina, which had by then become the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the remaining weapons were being removed from the positions and placed in depots and military installations that already existed by that time, and they were placed under so-called double key, under the supervision of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The arrival of the UNPROFOR, of the blue helmets, did it automatically mean an end to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all the citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I too hoped that the arrival of UN troops would bring peace to the area and a resolution of the political situation but that didn't happen. Raids, clashes, skirmishes continued, and we could say the aggression against that territory known already as the Republic of Serbian Krajina continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us of an instance of aggression that you are familiar with in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although it did not happen in the area that I was directly responsible for, it happened in an adjacent area, the municipality of Drnis. The Croatian army raided a UN protected area, UNPA, called the Miljevac plateau, just next to Benkovac municipality. They raided that municipality, captured a certain territory, and in that operation they killed around 50 members of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that situation, when UN troops called UNPROFOR had already been deployed together with the civilian police, what was the relationship between your public security station and the police of the RSK, on the one hand, to the UNPROFOR and the civilian police of the UN?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the CIVPOL and the UNPROFOR, our relations were good, they were welcomed very cordially, and we expected their assistance and help in ending the war and we also expected their protection from the Croatian army. At any rate, we expected an end to the war and a solution for the whole situation. The UNPROFOR was made up of parts of the French Battalion and the Kenyan Battalion, whereas members of the CIVPOL were of various nationalities but most of them at the time were from Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Vance Plan, on the basis of which UN troops were deployed in that area, did it envisage some sort of cooperation between the local police and the civilian police of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did. It envisaged cooperation in regulating the situation, protecting the whole population, supervision of the whole territory, patrolling, all these were supposed to be joint activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your area, the area of Benkovac municipality? How good was the cooperation of your local police with the civilian police of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment the UN civilian police station was established, our relationship with them was good. We had a good cooperation and we informed each other, although it was rather us who informed them, about the assignments we completed and activities and events that were taking place. We met at least once a week, I mean representatives of the police in Benkovac and the CIVPOL in Benkovac and once a week we submitted a report to the CIVPOL listing all events and developments for the past week, and if some serious crimes were involved, we would go further back than one week. We also listed our assignments and our performance in accomplishing these assignments. That section of the UNPROFOR covered Lika and Northern Dalmatia. In Sector South, we had meetings with the CIVPOL for Lika and Northern Dalmatia and we met in a different place every time to discuss the overall situation in the sector, and all chiefs of the civilian police, local police and all chiefs of the Sector South CIVPOL attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of any chief of CIVPOL from that area, from that sector, that you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived, members of the CIVPOL set up a number of those stations and later on, they streamlined a little but they had a permanent station in Knin, Kistanje, Benkovac, Obrovac, Drnis, Vrlika, and of course in the area of Lika, in places like Lapac, Korenica, Gracac and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained that you informed the civilian police of the United Nations on a regular basis. Did the UN civilian police have any obligations to notify or report to you? Was it a mutual thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for their obligations towards us, their only obligation was to pass information to us if anybody reported a crime to them, so that we would be able to take action. They sometimes got hold of information that was not available to us, and that happened mostly with reports made by Croatian citizens who would report incidents to them when they were on patrol. They had no other obligations towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the UN civilian police force have powers to conduct their own investigations on the ground, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what powers they had. They never told us. But I know that they usually asked us for information about various cases, what happened, what action was taken, whether that action was sufficient to detect the perpetrator. We always shared that information and always of course the ultimate objective was to apprehend the perpetrator, and all our work was geared at that. However, it was not always successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you describe your relationship with the civilian police of the UN and the UNPROFOR, and when I say "your," I mean the Benkovac public security station, was that relationship driven by your own personal attitude and approach, or did you have specific instructions on how to treat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had orders to establish cooperation with them, and I don't think it is my personal achievement in that area. It is a result of what we were asked to do, what we were instructed to do. The entire police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had the same instructions, to cooperate with the UN force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you to build up measures for protecting the Croat population in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meetings we had together and while analysing the situation in such areas and settlements, they asked us to strengthen controls and check-points. Yes, they often asked for that and we complied. We took such measures and we increased our presence in those settlements to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To protect that population from what? Can you tell us about specific villages and settlements where you did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like in every war, at that time, in the territory of Krajina, there were a lot of armed people, and discipline is weakened by the war. Individuals and groups would act on their own initiative, raiding, looting, even killing. Those were people, individuals, who were renegades, outlaws, people who thought that everything was permitted, and they took advantage of the situation when the police was not able to be everywhere and do everything. So they took law into their own hands, mostly for personal profits. They were mostly bandits and robbers. At that time, in the area of Benkovac municipality, we often had to protect people in Sopot, Dobropoljci, Perusic, both Gornji and Donji Perusic, Rodaljice, and later some smaller population centres where we set up check-points and built up patrols and increased our presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, before you proceed with the witness, and lest I forget, at page 10, line 20, you had posed this question to the witness: "Can you tell us the name of any chief of police from that area, from that sector, that you remember?" I believe the question was addressed in relation to Sector South. In addressing his answer, he said: "When they arrived, the members of CIVPOL set up a number of those stations" and later on he went on to list the stations involved. But he did not tell you the name of any chief. So I wondered if we could just deal with that answer which he overlooked to address specifically before you move on any further. Might I at this stage? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't notice that such a question was recorded in the transcript. The witness, in fact, answered the question that I actually asked. I asked him about the places where police stations were set up. It must be a misinterpretation, if that's what is recorded in the transcript. The witness anyway answered exactly what I asked. If you want me to ask him a question about chiefs, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, not at all. I was just addressing the question that was on the record. I am grateful for the opportunity to place the correct question on the record, on the transcript. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So that means there was no question asked about any chief of CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you understood correctly. At no point in time did I ask a question about the name of the chief of a UN civilian police station. What I did want to know is if the witness could tell us about the places where these stations were set up, to list the places for me, and I believe the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So are you saying that what is mentioned at page 10, line 20, that question is incorrect -- is incorrectly recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the correct question? Names of police stations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right. The question was the names of the police stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about these cases you've mentioned, renegades from law, bandits was the word you used, who for their own profit were attacking civilians? Did you look into such cases in your capacity as a police officer? Did you try to tackle any such incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the very description of our work as police officers that we have to investigate incidents and crimes like those. We acted in the spirit of those laws. We did our work as police officers all over the world do. There would be a report, the crime would be reported, we would go to the scene of crime, there would be an inspection, and whenever it was ascertained that a crime had been committed we would take steps to shed light on the circumstances and find the perpetrators as well as study the consequences of any crime. It was in fact the case that we had a number of serious crimes, murder more specifically, in Benkovac municipality. Civilians were murdered. Just after my arrival in Benkovac, sometime in April, in the village of Perusic Gornji, a woman named Peka [phoen] was murdered. I can't remember her family name. She read people's palms. That's what she was famous for. She was killed in her own home. Just after the crime became known, we took steps to inspect the crime scene and interview any witnesses. During our investigation, we found out that two young men, one from that village and one from the neighbouring village, had committed that crime. We started a pursuit and caught the perpetrators over the next two days. We brought them in, interviewed them, confiscated evidence such as a hunting rifle that they carried, and a pistol. We submitted this evidence to the relevant court for further processing. I know that they were later tried for this crime. Further, concerning more serious crimes, I remember that sometime in June 1992, a group of three perpetrators committed a quadruple murder of Croatian citizens in the village of Rodaljice. One lady survived, although they tried to kill her too but she survived. Having found out about that incident, we took appropriate steps and interviewed the surviving lady right away. She was able to identify one of the perpetrators. She gave us his name, and then we found another perpetrator, arrested them both, and brought them before an investigating magistrate. While this surviving lady was in hospital later on, she enjoyed full protection by the police, until the UN military component arrived in her village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in response to one of my previous questions you said you were upholding public law and order, and you were trying to tackle all the cases that came your way. Was this in fact more difficult due to the war that was on and how did the war make your work more difficult?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more difficult to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. The question is, once again, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Was this in fact more difficult due to the war that was on and how did the war make your war more difficult? You're telling him the answer. You are testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that wasn't the way I understood my own question. The witness previously answered that they had tried to tackle cases but this was made more difficult by the war, and I'm asking him why, to explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm quoting exactly what you said. Just look at page 15, line 24. I beg your pardon, line -- page 16, line 1. Was this in fact more difficult due to the war that was on and how did the war make your work more difficult? What better example of testifying can one get?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true. That is true, Your Honour. It's true. That's what it says. But I was referring to the witness's previous answer. He said that in as far as that was the case it was made more difficult, which is something the witness has said earlier. But I can rephrase my question, or perhaps I may as well give up the question so that it could not be construed as leading. I shall be asking further questions that I may be able to use in order to answer this one. My purpose was not to lead the witness but to take as some sort of a point of departure one of the witness's previous answers but this may be construed as leading and therefore I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Particularly when you don't say, "You told us previously A, B, C," you know, then we don't know where you come from. But we understand that may not have been your intention but it's the effect, you know. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could have a cite to the answer that the counsel is referring to, when he says that the witness previously testified about this. I just would be interested in the cite to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to show us that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just withdrawn the question. I see no point in pressing this matter any further. But if you insist, we can look at one of the previous questions or we can simply ask the witness to share that with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's look at it. Just show it to us. Because we want to see what is on the record, not what the witness is now going to say. We want to see what he has already said. Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't seem to be able to locate the exact point right now. I think that must have been about 15 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all the more important for you to link your question or your statement to what he said earlier, you know. Otherwise you sound like you're leading, and until we can find that, you are leading. Until we can find that previous statement, you really are leading, Mr. Milovancevic. You see, if you can just try to remind yourself all the time, not make statements, put a question: What happened, who did this, where did it happen, how did it happen? But once you start with any other word that is not why, who, when, how, you're likely to be asking -- making a -- asking a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let the record then show that you have not been able to show us that portion where he previously talked about the difficulty from the war. And you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a request to make, Your Honour. I would like to be given an opportunity after break to locate the exact point in the transcript for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what I've just been referring to, apparently, was said during private session so I violated a whole lot of things. May we just make sure that we edit away all of what I've just been saying right now. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 617 brought up on our screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the document appears, Witness, I can tell you that this is a summary report produced by the Benkovac public security station in relation to the period between the 10th of December and the 24th of December, 1991. You now have the document in front of you. What about the upper right corner of the document? Who submitted this report? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see in the heading is that the document was produced in the Benkovac public security station. It's about the area covered by the public security station between the 10th of December and the 24th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please for a moment look at page 2 of the document, the next page? The document only has two pages. Can you see who signed the document and what does the stamp tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was signed by Djuro Vukasinovic. At the time he was assistant chief in the crime department of the Benkovac public security station. The stamp reads: "Public security station, Ministry of Internal Affairs."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please now go back to page 1? There is reference there to a number of events, or, rather, crimes reported to the Benkovac public security station in this period, the first of these occurring on the 12th of December, 1991, and onwards. Do you see that report in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This document has been used before in these proceedings. If you look at the following date, the 21st of December, 1991, can you tell us what the report is about in relation to that particular date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. I think there is a lack of foundation for these questions. The witness has testified that he was not in Benkovac at this time period. So aside from just reading the document, which is already in evidence, I'm not sure if we have any basis for believing that the witness can contribute anything, if he has any knowledge that would elucidate this document beyond just reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall only be able to ascertain that once we have heard the witness's answer. The objection would be a logical one but only in case the Prosecutor knew already what I had in mind and what sort of question I would be asking. What I want to know is precisely what this document speaks about, what this document tells us about the situation that prevailed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is that this document is already in evidence. This witness was not in Benkovac around the dates of these events. He cannot speak to them other than to tell us what's already in the document, you know. Unless you say he drew this report and he was in Benkovac at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will ask -- I'm sorry if I interrupted. We will ask the witness what he knows about what is written in the document, if anything. I do not understand the misgivings of our colleague, Mr. Whiting, that there could be some prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- just to respond to that, I'm not concerned so much about prejudice as about relevance. And perhaps if the -- if the foundational questions were asked first; that is, do you know anything about what's written in this document; yes, I do; how do you know that -- or no, I don't. If yes, then how -- then how do you know it, and then proceed from there rather than skipping those questions and going right to asking him to comment. That's all that I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you with him now? You understand now his misgivings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, not at all, because the objection of my learned friend makes no sense. The witness did not write this document and I'm not going to ask him what's in the document because he's not the author, but I will ask him -- or, rather, I want to ask him if he knows anything about what -- about the events described in the document, the time when all that happened, about the war situation in that entire area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you can't want to have your cake and eat it. You're telling us -- listen to what you say. "The witness did not write this document and I'm not going to ask him what is in the document because he is not the author." Okay. Then you say: "But I will ask him -- or, rather, I want to ask him if he knows anything about what events -- about the events described in the document." Why do you -- you're contradicting yourself in the same sentence. Now, the objection is no foundation has been laid for the question that you want to ask, and the ruling is that, indeed, the objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the objection concerned the massacre in Bruska. With your leave, I would like to ask a different question related to this document. That's why I asked for it to be displayed on the screen, a different question, and I can lay the foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, lay the foundation. Let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when describing the end of 1991, you talked about the situation both in Knin and in Benkovac. Can you remind us once again what was that situation like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in the area of Knin, Benkovac and Obrovac, fighting was going on between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Croatian army, and the situation was very difficult. As for towns and villages on the front line itself and close to the front line, they were exposed to fire, both infantry fire and mortar fire, and artillery fire sometimes. As for towns like Benkovac, Obrovac and Knin, they were exposed to a large extent to artillery fire from tanks, rockets, mortars, multiple rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who -- where did that fire mostly come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read three lines, the fourth, fifth and the sixth date, the 21st, the 14th and the 22nd of December, 1991 in this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of December, 1991, around 2115 hours, an attack launched on Benkovac, shelling from a multiple rocket launcher. In -- later on on the same day, Stabanj fired upon by mortars. 14th of December, 1991 in the afternoon and evening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There must be something that I'm missing here or -- I really don't know. You have asked this witness to testify for the last couple of minutes about what he knew happening in Knin, Benkovac and Obrovac, and from there you just straight go into this document without laying foundation for asking questions on this document, and there is an objection standing on that. You've got to lay a foundation for using this document. What you were asking this person, this witness, has nothing to do with this document. Examples were given to you by the Prosecution: Do you know anything about these documents? If you do, how did you come to know? That's how you lay the foundation, Mr. Milovancevic. But you don't just get a witness who has nothing to do with this document to start talking about it and want to link what he has just been saying to this when there is no foundation for using this document. He's not the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reason why I asked those questions is the reply the witness gave me when I showed him the document, when he said he knew it, that it's from the public security of Benkovac, it bore the stamp, a signature, it's that it's the public security of Benkovac that made this report in end 1991 so he recognised the document. He acknowledged it. I went on to ask him if he were familiar with the general situation in that area. And now I want to compare that general situation with the description given in this document. And the witness is precisely reading sections from this document that tell us about the situation as it was in December 1992 -- 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I believe that misstates the evidence. The witness did not recognise the document. He read that the document was -- he recognised it as appearing to be a document from the public security section of Benkovac as it having the stamp from the public security section of Benkovac and being signed by an individual whom he described. All fine. But that's different from recognising the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I was going to try and say. All of us can read what's written there and the witness could -- that's what he did. He just read what's on the document, you know. And I don't know why Mr. Milovancevic is just refusing to ask these very basic questions that would lay the foundation for him to use this document. And I think I've given you examples of those questions. Mr. Whiting has also given those examples. Either you put that -- you made that foundation. If you don't make the foundation, I'm afraid, Mr. Milovancevic, we can't let you put questions about this document. Just lay the foundation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you see a stamp of the public security station on this document. Can you tell us whether public security stations in the Republic of Serbian Krajina or maybe SAO Krajina had the obligation to report all incidents and events that happened in the area that they covered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security stations were duty-bound and they had orders to report all major events that had a bearing on the security station to the SUP or a MUP of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Artillery fire on a town or any shooting that would happen in the area of responsibility of a public security station, was or was not an incident that had to be reported to a superior authority, the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bombing and shelling of population centres was always reported to superior command, and later on, such incidents were included in weekly or monthly reports that also made an analysis of the frequency, the incidence of such events and they were also submitted to the superior command. It was our obligation to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You read a report from the 21st of December about the shelling of Benkovac. You have another item concerning the 14th of December. Could you read that one, please? And that -- we'll finish with it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of December, 1991, in the afternoon and evening, mortars fired upon the area of Smilcici, Kasici, Zemunik Gornji, and Smokovic. All these are in the municipality of Benkovac, which is our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These reports about artillery activities in the territory of your municipality, what do they tell you? What was the situation like in the territory covered by the public security station of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports tell us that the situation was very difficult. Normal life was impossible. And normal work was impossible for members of the police force. Can you imagine members of the Ministry of the Interior who had to perform their jobs in Smilcici, Kasici and places like that, ten kilometres from the closest positions of the Croatian army, who were exposed to shelling while performing their daily duties? This was -- this had a bearing on their jobs and the tactics they employed in interviews aimed at detecting perpetrators. In the area of Benkovac municipality, as far as Croats are concerned, it was mainly the elderly people who remained in their homes. Younger members of their families had left for Zadar, Biograd and other places, and as the police performed their regular duties aimed at protecting the lives of the population, all the citizens of Benkovac, they would run into individual soldiers who quarrelled with them, who said, "Look at you, you are protecting Croats who live here, whereas other Croats at the other end of the front line keep shooting and shelling us." That's what I mean when I say that the job of a policeman was very difficult at that time. There were constant conflicts and the threat of a major conflict between the police and the army in the RSK, because the police was constantly subject to accusations that they were not sufficiently involved militarily and that they were protecting Croats, although they were just doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a short break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you some questions first? How was that when you arrived in Benkovac police station in April 1992 did you learn -- were you instructed about cases of serious crimes which happened before your arrival? And if yes, how were you instructed? How learned you about these cases? Especially cases where investigation had not been yet concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I arrived at Benkovac, the then chief of the public security station did not hand over his duties to me in the regular manner because he was on sick leave, absent from work, so I took over my duties with the help of other employees, other staff. They informed me about past events and incidents. I studied the archive of current case files that were in the police station. It was the duty of internal affairs organs, including the police station in Benkovac, to continuously work on investigation of crimes that have no statute of limitations, and war crimes and serious crimes like murder have no statute of limitations. So I familiarised myself with those cases with the help of my underlings. Some of those case files from the past period were resolved and closed. Some of them were pending, and I don't remember a particular case that we elucidated upon my arrival that had been pending from the past. But it is certain that a great number of crimes were elucidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What, according to your memory, was the most prominent cases? Do you not remember single cases from the couple of months before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that area before I arrived, there were several major crimes that I remember. For instance, one case when 10 inhabitants of a place called Bruska were killed. That happened in end 1991. I also remember a case when four or five people were killed in a place called Gornji Zemunik. That also happened a couple of months before my arrival. That perpetrator was found. And there were some other individual cases that my staff informed me about and we later established a link with other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just shortly about this case from Gornji Zemunik, who was the perpetrator who was found? Was that a single perpetrator, and who was it, of which ethnicity especially or was he or she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Gornji Zemunik, I remember that the victims were also from Gornji Zemunik. There were three or four elderly persons and the perpetrator was also a local, an ethnic Serb. I don't remember his name and surname, but I know that this was reported on TV, Krajina TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the victims also were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I mentioned that the victims were Croats, and the perpetrator was an ethnic Serb from the same village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And now about Bruska, these 10 inhabitants, were they also elderly persons, these victims? And also of Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, that happened one night in a house in Bruska. There was a total of 10 victims, nine of them Croats and one was a Serb. I think, if I can recall that now, that they were of differing age groups. I seem to remember that from the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Did you see also this report which we are having on our screen, or was this addressed to somebody else? Do you know that personally from your experience, after you arrived in Benkovac? Do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I was looking at a while ago is one of many documents that were being sent to Knin on a weekly basis. I had probably seen it in the archive in Benkovac at some point when I was going through the files to familiarise myself with the overall situation in Benkovac municipality. At the time, I could not really go into the substance of the report or whether it was truthful. This was a weekly report and there were many of those, most of which I went through at some time or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us how the investigation about this case of the massacre in Bruska went on under your guidance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I arrived in Benkovac about four or five months after this event had occurred. The distribution of forces on the ground I found was as follows: In Bruska there was a police station which was under the authority of the Benkovac public security station. This station was supposed to guard the remaining population in the area and to keep the situation under control. There was information to indicate that the massacre at Bruska had been committed by mistake by a Croatian sabotage forces that had been infiltrated into the area. There were all sorts of information circulating. Sometimes I would pass through the area and go to the Bruska station to see what was going on. The case was still open. And all the new information and new facts were being gathered and made up the relevant case file. Many things kept happening, new situations were emerging all the time. Some territories were falling, some were being taken by the Croatian forces in Benkovac municipality. There were a lot of things happening and I could not afford to focus on one thing alone. Rather, I worked on the most urgent cases. Whenever new information emerged from the previous period, cases could always be reopened. Had we had any kind of information at the time about the possible perpetrators, we certainly would have taken steps to shed light on that crime, whoever the perpetrators might have been. This was after all a crime where a large number of inhabitants from the same village had been killed in the same night, and that was a serious crime. I can also tell you about the problems we faced when some people were killed in the village of Dobropoljci, which is part of Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, thank you. I was just focusing on this case. Thank you very much for now. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the cases mentioned in this document on the screen be the kind of cases that you probably got familiar with as you arrived on the scene in -- at your new job in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I arrived in Benkovac, what I had to do was to survey the overall situation that I now found myself in and to consider the steps that were to be taken. On a daily basis, our soldiers and civilians were being killed on the ground. We tried to do our duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you? Could you please just concentrate on the question I put to you? Would the cases that you see mentioned on this document on the screen be the kind of cases that you became familiar with when you got to Benkovac? I think you can just say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, cases such as the one I have on my screen right now are the kind of cases that I first encountered when I came to work in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the document that is on the screen is the kind of document that constituted the reports that your police station generated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that you're looking at speaks about a 15-day period of time. The report was submitted to the superior command about events that had occurred over the previous period of time. This is a summary of those 15 days of that month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, just listen to my question. Is the document that you see on the screen the kind of document that was generated by your police station by way of reports that you had to make periodically? See, we don't have much time to hear a long story. When I ask you a question where you can answer either by yes or no, please just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would later send documents of this kind to our command. We would produce such documents and submit them to our command. These are summaries, but we would make special detailed files in relation to each of the crimes and incidents that occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in one of your previous answers you mentioned an act of aggression around the Miljevac plateau, which was an area adjacent to yours, to the area in which you worked. During your time at the Benkovac public security station, were there any acts of aggression against your own area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I have to interrupt you now. Your Honours, we might want to redact the first part of the sentence, the beginning of the witness's answer, where the witness identifies himself. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We must strike off what you've just said too. Page 32, line 22, 11 or whatever that is, can that please be deleted, as well as page 33, line 3, 11.09.15. Mr. Milovancevic, I think -- I thought Judge Hoepfel was trying to lay the foundation for you to use this document. Are you going to go back to this document or are you done with it, this document that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That in fact was the sense of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in addition to all the answers we have received, the Defence has no need to go back to this document since it has already been tendered and admitted. That is the reason why I chose not to dwell on the matter. I believe Your Honour, Judge Hoepfel, has shed sufficient light on all the facts surrounding this document. That's our position, and that's why I chose not to go back to the document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we can get it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You started explaining about the situation in Benkovac itself. Will you please repeat your answer, since we had to interrupt the proceedings in order to protect your identity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January, 1993 an act of aggression was committed against Benkovac municipality, more specifically the following villages: Islam, Grcki, Hasic, Smokovic, by the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any UN troops deployed in the area and how long did the aggression last? How long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a UN presence in the area, more specifically the military component. Part of the UN French Battalion were deployed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about the impact of that attack? What exactly happened in Benkovac and its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the attack was quite sudden. In the morning hours on January 22nd, just after daybreak, at about half past 6.00 or quarter to 7.00 in the morning. At first there was shelling of these villages by artillery fire and then the Croatian infantry forces moved in. The population was not enjoying any protection from its own army. There was some UNPROFOR check-points in the area but the population remained unprotected. They suffered a lot of casualties. They arose from their beds and tried to escape and flee to Benkovac in a bid to save their lives. As for the town itself, a great confusion and panic reigned. It was necessary to mobilise new forces and send them immediately to the front line. People and refugees were already arriving in the town, the inhabitants of those surrounding villages. Horrible news spread of many killed and the situation was becoming increasingly difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about refugees and civilians, can you tell us which ethnic group these people belonged to and where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The refugees arriving from those villages were ethnic Serbs because those villages were ethnically Serb villages, and all the refugees were Serbs who had been attacked by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this situation that arose in January 1993, did you receive any orders from Mr. Martic, the then Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first order I received at the time from the military command based in Benkovac was to use our police forces to defend the Pridraga-Novi Grad axis which is near a place called Karin, the reason being the army did not have sufficient forces at its disposal to cover the entire length of the front line so we sent all of our police to that area, with very few police officers remaining in town for various emergencies. At the time, I remember receiving a phone call from Minister Martic asking me to get in touch with the Kenya Battalion and try to work with them to evacuate some UNPROFOR soldiers left behind in Karin and Zemunik Gornji. Karin is a sea-coast settlement near a Catholic monastery. There was a rather small unit of UNPROFOR's FrenchBat stationed there. Amid all the fighting, several Croat shells landed on the French camp, killing three French soldiers. The remaining soldiers there were now blocked and could not leave the area. My order was to help lift the blockade and help them leave the area, in cooperation with the commander of the Kenya Battalion, an interpreter and a number of other people that I'm unable to specify right now, some people from his escort, some of his associates, we left in the evening and helped to evacuate the remaining elements of the unit alongside with their equipment from that camp. They withdrew to their own headquarters in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a while? You said you helped get the rest of the unit evacuated. Whose unit was this? Who were you helping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've mentioned before, I was helping members of UNPROFOR's FrenchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to identify the area in which all of this is taking place and since there has been mention of a great number of villages and settlements, I think it might be useful for the witness to show us on the ELMO, on page 25 of the atlas. Mine is marked so if the usher could please give me a hand with this, if there is a blank copy of the atlas, an unmarked copy of the atlas maybe that could be handed to the witness so he can show us where these villages are. I'm talking about page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is loaded in e-court, so I think actually it can be accessed by e-court and marked that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we please have it coming up on the screen then from the e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's document 23, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think because it's such a big document it takes a few seconds for it to come up but I believe it will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this document appears on our screens, not to waste time, Witness, let me ask you about this instruction you received from Mr. Martic regarding the rescue of UNPROFOR troops. What was the situation with the civilian police in that area? What were your duties regarding them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the civilian police of the United Nations, in this aggression against Ravni Kotari, which is the name of that area in Benkovac, they were taken by surprise, too, and they found themselves in a difficult situation. There was a great inflow of refugees from afflicted villages, and those refugees were very aggressive because their friends and family had been killed and because they were driven out without being able to take any belongings and they were very aggressive also because they believed that under the resolution UN troops were supposed to protect those UNPAs and there were rumours that members of the French Battalion cooperated with Croatian forces and had helped them mount this operation by removing mines and pointing out the minefields that stood between Croatian forces and these areas. So as I said, these refugees were very angry and aggressive and they -- there was an attack against the station of the CIVPOL, so I sent my men to protect that station because UN civilian police were not armed and some of the attackers were armed. And they urged each other to shoot. That's why I asked the deputy of the police station in Benkovac to help this, to help in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I stop you here, Witness? Did Mr. Martic give you any orders regarding the position of the civilian police at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for orders given at that time, it was said in a telephone conversation that members of the United Nations, both of the military mission and the CIVPOL must be kept absolutely safe because they were not responsible for the aggression. And I was asked to evacuate UN representatives from Karin and Zemunik and to protect CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did you evacuate them and did you protect them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conjunction with them, because I went immediately to their hotel to see them, we decided on a course of action because they didn't have any instructions from their superiors on what to do and how to behave. Some of them had private accommodation, some of them were living in the hotel, and I told them that they should all move to the hotel where I would give them police and military security so that nobody could come near them to endanger them, and they would have 24-hour security from the MUP of the Serbian Krajina, and if they needed to go to their apartments to fetch something, they would get police escort until they returned to the hotel. And they continued to live in the hotel and to be fed there and have normal communications with their command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness, were these UNPROFOR people in a hotel or in a Catholic monastery? I thought I heard you earlier talk of a Catholic monastery, unless I misheard it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I spoke about the Catholic monastery, I meant members of the military mission of the French Battalion. That monastery was in Donji Karin, a place where three members of the UNPROFOR were killed. But that was the military component of the UN mission, French people. And my second answer, the second part of my answer, referred to the civilian police of the UNPROFOR, and those are two different cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we zoom in on quadrant 2 on the monitor? Raise the document a little to see Zadar and the hinterland of Zadar. Further up, please. I don't know if I'm clear. Scroll in the other direction. Good. Good. We can leave it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want Zadar or Knin? I see Zadar has disappeared from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's why it would have been better perhaps to put the atlas on the ELMO before the witness. Because Zadar is on page 24, and in the electronic system the atlas is divided into pages, so you can't see two pages at the same time, although those are adjacent areas, or maybe we can. Yes, perfect. Leave it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you use the pencil that the usher will give you now to show us what places were attacked, their juxtaposition to Benkovac, which villages were in danger.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January, 1993, the following places were attacked: Latinski Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you underline these places? Just underline or make a little circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Islam Grcki. We can't see Kasic village, which is here. And there is another place, Gornji Zemunik. And Smokovic, just below the airport, Smokovic village. Those were the villages that were attacked on the 22nd January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the members of the French Battalion to whom you extended assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donji Karin was here, and the Croat forces, attacking along this axis, soon emerged at Novi Grad and the Novi Grad sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you encircle Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here in Gornji Zemunik there were also members of the UNPROFOR whom we pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you also encircle Benkovac to see where you were located? Thank you. From what villages did refugees come to Benkovac? Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same morning, and that continued until noon, a large number of refugees arrived from Latinski Islam, although fewer of them because that village had been destroyed in previous operations and it was a mixed -- it used to be a mixed village. And the Croats had fled in the first part of the war, and now Serbs had to pull out. In Grcki Islam, the population was purely Serb. In Kasic village, the population also fled to Benkovac. And of course, the population of Smokovic village and some from Gornji Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this is too early. Can I leave this map on the monitor for the time being, if we need the witness to show some more locations, and I will tender it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is in your hands, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long these combat operations lasted? Was it just on the 22nd January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat operations in that area lasted intensively for about two and a half months on a daily basis. There was a great number of casualties, and I can say that every day on the Serb side we had 10 to 15 dead, mostly soldiers but some civilians as well, who got killed in the shelling of both military and civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you, did you mean every day during those two and a half months while the combat lasted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For that entire period. I remember well some conversations when I arrived at Benkovac, at that time there were around 100 of inhabitants of Benkovac who had been killed in combat, in which they were involved on the side of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. During this operation that was called Maslenica 3, there were about 420 or 430 dead, including the hundred from the past period, and a large number of the casualties were natives of other parts of Serbian Krajina and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned this figure, 420 or 430, what is that figure? I don't think it's clear from the record. I don't think it's clear from your answer. What does that figure represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That figure, 420, is the number of army troops who were killed from the beginning of the war until April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that the Croatian attack was sudden, that the army gave you an assignment to mobilise police officers who would help out on the front line. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you organise yourselves to maintain public order and law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, law and order was not a -- the priority. The priority was to preserve our territory, to preserve as much of the territory as we could and to stop the Croatian forces from advancing. That was our priority task, and everything else was -- came second. Mobilisation of policemen and everything else came later. Those were all assignments that we had to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any volunteers in that territory at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were various units of volunteers in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the fighting stopped? Who stopped this Croatian attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, the Croatian attack was stopped by the army of Serbian Krajina. And then a line was established, a line of clash, of fighting, and fighting continued every day. This conflict was terminated, thanks to an agreement whose name I don't remember now. I think it was the Zagreb agreement. But it was an agreement between the warring parties under the aegis of the UNPROFOR. A cease-fire was agreed along with a number of other things, such as withdrawal of the Croatian troops from territories they had captured, return of refugees to those territories, et cetera, and that agreement had a number of others provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened with these villages that the Croatian attack was directed at in this Maslenica 3 operation? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several months later, in April or May 1993, and even later, the inhabitants of those villages would occasionally go to visit their homes in that area. I, too, visited occasionally. And I can say that all the houses and property were destroyed and burned, and the houses were no longer fit to live in, and due to a large number of mines and unexploded devices, it was unsafe to live there, and there were many cases, accidents, that happened when people came to visit their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In all that time, while the fighting lasted, how did the population of Benkovac live and behave, including the refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb refugees from those villages that I just mentioned found accommodation in Benkovac and the surrounding area, whereas another part went on to Knin and the Knin area, where they resettled. They were unhappy, extremely unhappy, and they threatened to fight and use their weapons. They blamed UN troops for all that had happened to them and they also blamed our military command in Benkovac, who put their trust in the UNPROFOR and agreed to withdraw into their barracks and place their weaponry under double lock. They were furious over all that had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the native Croatian population in Benkovac and other areas? Did they experience any difficulty in the course of this operation, in the course of Operation Maslenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic Croats who remained in Benkovac itself and its surroundings, and I later heard that this was the case in Knin and other villages around Knin such as Vrpolje, were experiencing some degree of difficulty because Serb refugees would come to their homes and take their homes by force, move in by force, in order to have somewhere to stay, a roof over their heads. In both Benkovac and Knin, there were very few police officers remaining in the area to uphold law and order and to deal with the sort of problems that the police usually have to deal with, that constitute usual police work. There were problems along the front near Pridraga and Novi Grad. Our priority was to protect our territory. Internal trouble was less important since we believed to have the protection of our territory as our upper most priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to deal with the problem with the existing forces, the forces that you had? How did you go about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had few people and the problems were mounting which made our work very difficult, needless to say, especially in view of the fact that we had been asked and there had been an order from the military command in Benkovac to help the military police with mobilising new soldiers. We had to tour all the villages in a bid to mobilise all able-bodied men in order to get them to join the army. We were facing the difficulty with accommodating all the refugees. The town was being shelled on a daily basis by artillery fire, by multiple rocket launchers. Another problem was the fact that we had to protect the Croats living in the area, lest they be subjected to acts of revenge by individuals or people who might have had some hidden intentions. All of this had to be done. We had a Crisis Staff set up in Benkovac for these purposes. Their aim was to help with putting up refugees who were being put up in kindergarten, school buildings and other public institutions. Some Croats came, most of them elderly people. They were afraid for their lives, and they said that they would rather move out of the Benkovci area and go to Zadar and they needed help with this. They applied to the Red Cross to move out of the Benkovac area and to be sent to Zadar where some younger members of their own families were staying. The Crisis Staff drew up a list and organised a convoy for these people. Most of the remaining Croats left the Benkovac area after Maslenica 93 operation. Very few Croats remained, a mere handful of them. Certainly less than were present in the area before the operation. They left on that convoy. I remember that because I assigned some escort to that convoy to keep any loose cannons from committing acts of massacre against the civilian population. The escort followed them as far as the Zemunik airport which was the confrontation line and that was where they crossed to the other side and that's how the situation ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your last reply, if I may just ask you something, is this some sort of understated expulsion, if I may put it that way, or secret expulsion or covert expulsion? Do you think this operation could be termed an act of covert expulsion by the Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no way that anyone could describe this as an organised way of expelling people from Benkovac municipality. There can be no talk of that. I would even go as for as to say that we helped these people, because many of them could have fallen prey to bandits and gangs roaming the area because this is precisely the sort of situation that is quite common in a war. All the systems of state control are weakened and such individuals, rampaging individuals, enjoy a greater degree of freedom. I'm sure that we -- or I managed to save a great many lives by evacuating those people. We took all the steps necessary, although we were facing a great deal of pressure along the front line and elsewhere, but we assigned forces to this mission in order to have it successfully implemented and in order to get these people out alive and perhaps make a future return for them possible, which later proved to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While describing this situation about the Croatian aggression early in 1993, you described how you treated the civilian police. During this trial we have heard evidence and we have seen documents that could lead us to conclude that the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was making the work of the civilian police impossible. Do you know anything to indicate such a conclusion, and can you draw a link between what I've just told you and the situation as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of any such reports, such as the ones you've mentioned. At no point in time, not even after work resumed at the civilian police station did we hear any such reports from them. Once the situation was normalised in the area, they returned and we resumed work and we picked up where we had left off. We used to meet a lot. We used to talk about things, and I never heard anything being said by them about their work being made difficult or impossible. I will tell you about a situation that I faced myself, when I helped protect and preserve members of the civilian police in Benkovac on the 22nd of January, 1993. They had spent several days in a hotel there until they were ordered to go back to their headquarters in Knin. There was a news flash on CNN that the local police chief had taken hostage a number of UNPROFOR civilian police officers. I'm not sure who was the first to break the news or for what reason, but I know that two or three days later, Cedric Thornberry arrived in Benkovac, who at the time was a high-ranking UNPROFOR official in Yugoslavia. He came to see for himself what was going on. He talked to members of the civilian police who told him that they were never held hostage, they were merely arrested for a short while, and they thanked him for coming. Most of the UN civilian police returned to Benkovac later on and they resumed work as usual until the very end of their mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the Benkovac public security station for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to work there until the 1st of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that Mr. Martic became president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic became president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in April 1994, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you say you were still at the Knin public security station. Do you know anything about the position taken by Mr. Martic as president of the republic, his position on the crimes committed and their perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was all the time in touch with Mr. Martic, and whenever we met at meetings, and whenever police work was discussed, especially whenever there were any celebrations such as the Krajina Police day on the 4th of July or the 5th of July. The 5th of July was security day in Krajina. Mr. Martic would address police officers and citizens to express his best wishes, and he always remained adamant that we should act in accordance with the laws and that we should try to be as successful as possible and get the best possible results in our work. This was not mere lip service in his case. His support meant more in purely practical terms, where he clearly demonstrated that he meant what he was saying. I can't be specific about the date, but I know that this happened after Maslenica 93 operation. Martic once ordered that all perpetrators of serious crimes be arrested, particularly murderers. These perpetrators were then tried, but for a variety of reasons these people were not detained in prison but were eventually released. The fact that such people were being released caused shock among the honest people of Krajina. They asked that these persons be isolated and be sent where they belonged, but the judicial bodies, for all sorts of reasons, both objective and subjective, neglected their duties and failed to carry out their tasks, which left Mr. Martic with no choice but to issue an order to that effect. I remember we were in Benkovac municipality, and our mission was to arrest such people and take them to be locked up in prisons near Stara Gradiska and Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the name of Sameer Bino; does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
